title: Decorators
blurb: Functions that wrap functions: transparent pass-through, preserved identity, and state carried on the wrapper.

cells.title: @ is a rebinding, nothing more
cells.body:
A decorator is just a function that takes a function and returns a function. The @ line is pure sugar: @emphasize
def note(): ... means note = emphasize(note) — call the decorator with the function object, then rebind the name to whatever comes back. Once you see that, decorators stop being magic and become ordinary higher-order functions you can write, test and debug by hand.

The reasoning habit: after decoration, the name refers to the wrapper, not the original. Every call through the name goes through the wrapper; the original function survives only if the wrapper's closure kept a reference to it. That is simultaneously the power (a seam where you can add behavior) and the hazard (forget to call the original and you silently break the function).

cells.title: Be a transparent wrapper
cells.body:
A good wrapper is invisible to its callers: it accepts whatever arguments the wrapped function accepts and returns what it returns, unchanged except for the added behavior. The tool for that is *args, **kwargs in the wrapper signature, forwarded verbatim to the wrapped call — hard-coding one parameter works for one function but breaks the moment the decorator decorates anything else.

The other half of transparency is identity. By default, the decorated name loses its __name__ and __doc__ (they now belong to the wrapper). functools.wraps(func) copies them over, so introspection, help output and debug logs keep showing the real function. 'Wrap generically, restore identity' is the difference between a toy decorator and one you can ship.

cells.title: Wrappers that remember things
cells.body:
Function objects can carry attributes, and a wrapper is a function object — so it can own state. Set wrapper.calls = 0 before returning it, increment it inside, and suddenly every decorated function keeps its own call counter. The same mechanism holds caches: a dict attribute keyed by the arguments turns any pure function into a memoizing one, with no globals and no classes.

Each application of the decorator creates a fresh wrapper with fresh attributes, which is exactly the isolation you want: two functions decorated by the same @count_calls count separately. This is how instrumentation (hit counters, timers), caching, and access control are built in the wild — behavior added at the seam, state owned by the wrapper, the original function untouched.

exercise.title: Shout It
exercise.statement:
A stadium scoreboard API returns polite lowercase strings, and the big screen wants them LOUD. Write the decorator shout(func): it wraps a one-argument function that returns a string, and the wrapper returns the original result uppercased with an exclamation mark appended — "hi ada" becomes "HI ADA!". Use functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its identity.

Then write the tested driver shout_report(names): inside it, define greet(name) returning "hi " + name, decorate it with @shout, call it once per name, and return [results, greet.__name__] — the list of shouted results plus the function's name, which proves the identity survived the wrapping.
constraints: names contains 0 to 50 strings, possibly empty strings
greet is exactly 'hi ' + name — do not change it
the decorator must work on ANY one-argument function returning a string, not just greet

examples.why: each result is uppercased with a bang, and the name is still 'greet' thanks to wraps
no names, but the identity check still runs

exercise.starter:
import functools


def shout(func):
    """Decorate a one-arg str->str function: uppercase + '!'."""
    pass


def shout_report(names):
    """Decorate greet with @shout and report results + greet.__name__."""
    pass
hints: What two strings do you have to combine in the wrapper — and in which order relative to calling the original function?
wrapper(name) returns func(name).upper() + '!'. Decorate wrapper with functools.wraps(func) before returning it, or greet.__name__ will be 'wrapper'.
Inside shout_report: define greet with @shout above it, build [greet(n) for n in names], and return [that list, greet.__name__].
exercise.reasoning: The wrapper adds behavior at exactly one seam: between the original function's return and the caller. Getting func(name).upper() + "!" right is the trivial half; the teaching half is identity. Without functools.wraps, the name greet is rebound to the wrapper, so greet.__name__ reports "wrapper" — debug logs, tracebacks and documentation tools all silently lie. With it, the metadata is copied and the function looks untouched from the outside. 'Change the behavior, preserve the identity' is the contract every production decorator honors.

exercise.title: Every Call Counts
exercise.statement:
Ops wants a usage meter on every endpoint: each decorated function should know how many times it has been called. Write the decorator count_calls(func): the returned wrapper forwards any arguments to the original and maintains a .calls attribute on itself — 0 at the moment of decoration, one more after every call.

Then write the tested driver echo_report(script): define echo(x) returning x * 2, decorate it with @count_calls, and return [before, outs, after] — the counter value before any call, the list of echo(x) results for the script in order, and the counter value after.
constraints: the wrapper must accept any *args/**kwargs, not just one argument
the counter starts at 0 the instant the decoration happens, before any call

examples.why: fresh counter reads 0, three calls double three values, then it reads 3
an empty script never calls echo

exercise.starter:
import functools


def count_calls(func):
    """Wrap func with a .calls counter starting at 0."""
    pass


def echo_report(script):
    """Decorate echo with @count_calls; return [before, results, after]."""
    pass
hints: Where can a counter live so that each decorated function gets its own, and so that the wrapper can update it on every call?
Set wrapper.calls = 0 right before returning the wrapper (that is when 'decoration happened'). Inside, do wrapper.calls += 1 and then return func(*args, **kwargs).
In the driver: before = echo.calls, then outs = [echo(x) for x in script], then return [before, outs, echo.calls]. Reading before any call is what proves the counter starts at zero.
exercise.reasoning: Function attributes are the quiet feature doing all the work here: wrapper.calls is per-decoration state — every function wrapped by count_calls gets its own counter, because each application of the decorator builds a new wrapper object with a fresh attribute. The [before, ..., after] shape of the driver is deliberate: reading the counter before any call pins down the initialization contract (0 at decoration time), while the after value pins the increment contract (one bump per call, arguments irrelevant). Instrumentation that can prove both properties is instrumentation you can trust on a dashboard.

exercise.title: The Receipt Cache
exercise.statement:
A pricing service computes quotes with a slow lookup, and the same item is priced again and again. Build a memoizing decorator memoize(func) by hand — a plain dict attribute on the wrapper as the cache; functools.lru_cache and every other caching helper are off the table, the point is to build the machinery yourself.

The wrapper must expose two counters alongside the cache: .calls — how many times the wrapper was invoked — and .misses — how many times the wrapped function actually had to run (a cache miss). Then write the tested driver cost_report(script): define cost_of(n) returning 3 * n + 1, decorate it with @memoize, run the whole script, and return [results, cost_of.calls, cost_of.misses]. If the cache works, repeated arguments drive a wedge between calls and misses.
constraints: script contains 0 to 100 integers between -50 and 50
the cache is a plain dict living on the wrapper; no functools.lru_cache or imported caching
counters start at 0; every hit is a call that is not a miss

examples.why: three calls, but only the first 4 and the 5 were misses — the second 4 was served from the cache
a single fresh argument is one call and one miss

exercise.starter:
import functools


def memoize(func):
    """Cache results in a plain dict on the wrapper.

    The wrapper exposes .calls (invocations) and .misses (times the
    wrapped function actually ran). No functools.lru_cache allowed.
    """
    pass


def cost_report(script):
    """Decorate cost_of with @memoize; return [results, calls, misses]."""
    pass
hints: What should the cache be keyed on so that two calls 'with the same input' hit, and what must you check BEFORE calling the wrapped function?
Key the dict by the argument tuple. In the wrapper: bump .calls; if the key is absent, bump .misses, run the function, and store the result; return the stored value either way.

wrapper.cache = {}, wrapper.calls = 0, wrapper.misses = 0 at decoration time. Inside: key = args (a one-arg function makes this simple); if key not in wrapper.cache: wrapper.misses += 1 and wrapper.cache[key] = func(*args). Return wrapper.cache[key].
exercise.reasoning: Memoization is one conditional wrapped around one dictionary lookup, and the two counters make its economics observable: calls - misses is the hit count, the number of expensive computations you actually avoided. The ordering inside the wrapper is the correctness core — check the cache before running the function, store on a miss, and return the cached value in both paths — get the order wrong and you either never hit or never populate. Note the precondition the whole design rests on: the wrapped function must be pure (same arguments, same result). Decorate something with side effects or time-dependent output and the cache serves convincing wrong answers, which is exactly why lru_cache is applied deliberately and sparingly in real codebases.
